🧰 Use AI well · Step 3 of 4 · 5 min

A tutor, not a ghostwriter

Requests that make you better, and honest use at school.

✍️ Two ways to use a chatbot for learning

You can use a chatbot as a ghostwriter: someone who writes instead of you. You type “Write my essay”, and a finished text appears. Now you have a text, but your brain has had almost no practice.

Or you can use it as a tutor: a teacher who works with one student at a time, asks questions, gives hints and explains mistakes. You type “Ask me questions until I understand.”

The second way is slower. But it is the one that builds your own skill, because the thinking stays with you.

Sometimes you only need a result: a packing list for a trip, a name for a pet. Then it is fine to let a chatbot do the work. Here we talk about the times when the goal is to learn.

Task. Tutor or ghostwriter? What does each request turn the chatbot into?

Show the solution

After a tutor request the thinking is still yours: you solve, you answer, you correct. After a ghostwriter request the thinking has been done for you, and all that is left is to copy.

💭 The trap: reading feels like knowing

A chatbot usually explains clearly, and its answer comes in seconds. You read it, every step makes sense, and it feels as if you know the topic now.

But following someone else's steps is much easier than finding them yourself. So this feeling can trick you, and it has a name: the illusion of knowing.

There is an honest test. Close the chat, then explain the topic or solve a similar task from memory. What you can do without looking is what you really know.

This is why this site asks you a question after each new idea, and brings some questions back days later.

Task. You read a chatbot's clear explanation, and everything seems obvious. How can you find out whether you have really learned it?

Show the answer

Right answer: Close it and explain the idea from memory, in your own words

Only a try without the answer in front of you shows what you can really do. Rereading makes the text familiar, and familiar feels like known: this is the illusion of knowing. The chatbot cannot look into your head, and a saved chat keeps the knowledge in the chat, not in your memory.

🧰 Three requests that turn a chatbot into a tutor

Copy one, put your own words in place of the square brackets and try it. If the chatbot still tells you too much, write back: “Only a hint, please.”

Even as a tutor, a chatbot can make mistakes. If a hint or a correction looks strange, check it in your textbook or ask your teacher.

Task. What does each request give you?

Show the solution

Four kinds of help, and none of them does the work for you. After an explanation, remember the honest test: close it and say the idea in your own words.

🤝 Honest use

Rules about AI differ from school to school, from job to job and even from task to task. One teacher lets you ask a chatbot for comments on your draft. Another wants you to write the whole essay with no AI at all.

Three questions help you each time:

1. Is it allowed here? If you do not know, ask.
2. Can I say openly how I used it? For example: “A chatbot quizzed me before the test.”
3. Is the work I hand in really mine? The words and the main ideas should be yours.

If you want to hide how you used AI, that is a warning sign.

Task. Your teacher has not said whether you may use AI for an essay. What is the honest thing to do?

Show the answer

Right answer: Ask the teacher first, and then say openly how you used it

When a rule is not clear, the honest thing is to ask, not to decide for the teacher. If AI is allowed, say openly how it helped: then you have nothing to hide. Staying silent, changing a few words and using it secretly have one thing in common: you hope the teacher will not find out.

Think first. A chatbot can write an essay in less than a minute. What do you lose if you let it?

Show the answer

The practice. At school the essay itself was never the goal. The goal is what happens in your head while you write: you find out what you want to say, choose the words and notice what you do not understand yet.

A text that you did not write gives you none of this.

And one day you will need the skill itself: in an exam, at a job interview, in a real conversation. No chatbot will do the thinking for you there.

Task. You have a hard problem to solve and a chatbot that can help. Put the steps in the order that teaches you the most.

Show the solution
  1. Try to solve the problem yourself, without the chatbot
  2. Ask for one hint about the place where you got stuck
  3. Finish the solution yourself, using the hint
  4. Ask the chatbot to check your finished solution and explain any mistakes

Your own try shows exactly where you are stuck, so a small hint is often enough to get you past that place. The check comes last, when there is a finished solution of your own. Asking for the answer at the start would skip every step that teaches you.

Task. Which request makes a chatbot work as a tutor?

Show the answer

Right answer: “Ask me questions about the water cycle, one at a time, and correct my answers.”

Only the request for questions leaves the work to you: you recall, you answer, and the chatbot corrects you. The other three ask for something finished: a report, a summary, the answers. You would get a text, but no practice.

Remember

  • A chatbot can be a tutor or a ghostwriter. A tutor request leaves the thinking to you, and that is what builds your skill.
  • Reading a clear answer feels like knowing: this is the illusion of knowing. So test yourself: close the chat and explain the topic from memory.
  • Three tutor requests: “A hint, not the answer”, “Quiz me” and “Check my explanation”.
  • Honest use: it is allowed, you can say openly how you used AI, and the work you hand in is really yours.
